blocks.text: CHAPTER TWENTY-THREE MENTAL HEALTH CONDITIONS
Aggressive Disruptive Behaviors in Adults

Agitation may escalate to overt aggression and often manifests with restlessness, pacing, and loud or demanding speech. Aggressive behavior includes verbally abusive language, specific verbal threats, intimidating physical behavior, and/or actual physical violence to self, others or property. All agitation and aggression must be considered an emergency and violence prevented wherever possible.

blocks.text: Causes:
Physical: acute medical illness, delirium and its causes, epilepsy, intracerebral lesions, traumatic brain injury.
Psychiatric: psychosis, mania, agitated depression, neurocognitive disorders, developmental disorders, severe anxiety.
Substance misuse: alcohol, cannabis, methaqualone (mandrax) intoxication or withdrawal; stimulant (e.g. cocaine) intoxication; benzodiazepine withdrawal.

Psychological factors: high levels of impulsivity and antagonism, hypersensitivity to rejection or insult, poor frustration tolerance and maladaptive coping skills all contribute to aggression and rage

blocks.text: In pregnant women: labour, obstetric complications, sepsis, organ failure as well as substances and mental disorders
Non-Pharmacological Management
Before starting pharmacological treatment, conduct a structured assessment:
Explore possible reasons for their distress
Check for and address clinical or environmental causes (e.g., pain, delirium, or inappropriate care).
Ensure the safety of the patient and those caring for them.
Caution is needed with elderly and frail patients as they are vulnerable to falls and further injury if sedated.

The use of physical restraint should only be employed when there is a need to protect the patient and surrounding people in an acute setting and it should be for as short time as possible with a constant monitoring of patients’ safety. Manual restraint may be necessary to administer medication.

safety. Manual restraint may be necessary to administer medication.

blocks.text: Mechanical restraint: Only if absolutely necessary to protect the patient and others for as short a time as possible.
Document the type, sites and duration of any restraints used.
15-minute monitoring: vital signs, the mental state, restraint sites, and reasons for use.
As initial and ongoing management, offer psychosocial and environmental interventions to reduce aggressive and disruptive behavior.
De-escalation Techniques should be attempted first:
Be calm, confident, kind, and reassuring.
Maintain a submissive posture with open hands.
Do not turn your back on the patient; avoid direct eye contact.

runs.text: Do not turn your back on the patient; avoid direct eye contact.

blocks.text: Do not attempt to reason with the patient.
Do not argue, confront delusions, or touch the patient.
Set clear limits regarding behavior.
Take patient to quiet, calm area – do not leave unobserved
Note: In Pregnant women:
Never leave unattended.
Use restraint sparingly, with care, if possible, with mother in a supported semi-seated position (not supine or prone).

AND

OR

If haloperidol is unavailable,
A: chlorpromazine (deep IM) 25–50mg may be repeated as necessary 4 times in 24hours (Maximum dose: 2000mg per 24hours).
If patient is known to suffer from schizophrenia and is not neuroleptic naïve give:
S: zuclopenthixol acetate IM) 50–150 mg (Repeat after 2–3 days, if necessary.
Give a maximum of 3 repeat injections and should not be used for longer than 2 weeks. The maximum administered dose should not exceed 400mg.
If patient develops acute dystonia give:
A: promethazine (deep IM) 25–50 mg 24hourly. In the elderly 25 mg (Maximum dose: 100mg per 24hours.
OR

OR
A: atropine (IM) 0.5 -2 mg when required
Note
Repeated doses of high potency antipsychotics may lead to the development of the life- threatening neuroleptic malignant syndrome. If suspected, stop antipsychotic, and institute supportive care.

blocks.text: Delirium

Delirium or acute confusion state is a condition characterized by disturbance in attention accompanied with reduced awareness of the environment; develops over a short period of time and fluctuates in severity.

runs.text: awareness of the environment; develops over a short period of time and fluctuates in severity.

Inability to stay focused on a topic or to switch topics

Non-Pharmacological Management
Control the acute disturbance.
Patients who actively walk with symptoms of agitation or restlessness require close observation within a safe and reasonably closed environment.

Firstly, attempts should be made to identify and remedy possible causes of agitation, e.g. pain, thirst, or a need for the toilet.
